problem: Prior VLM-based navigation either relies on modular pipelines (3D mapping, planner, low-level policy) that are complex and task-specific, or prompts VLMs naively, where they fail at fine-grained spatial outputs, obstacle avoidance and exploration. PIVOT, the closest visual-prompting baseline, ignores depth/feasibility and needs many VLM calls per action.
motivation: Navigation contains much reasoning similar to image question answering, where VLMs excel, so recasting it as a QA problem could yield a general zero-shot end-to-end policy for any vision-based navigation task. Doing so requires giving the VLM feasible, well-spaced, exploration-biased action choices grounded visually in the image.
key_idea: Turn navigation into image question-answering by projecting a small set of collision-free, exploration-biased action options as numbered arrows onto the RGB image and letting an off-the-shelf VLM pick one in a single call, with a separate VLM call for stopping.
insight: Choosing the action candidates (navigability from depth plus explore bias) matters most: on ObjectNav, Ours 50.4% SR vs 33.2% for Ours w/o nav (evenly spaced arrows) vs 29.8% Prompt Only. Visual annotation mostly improves efficiency (SPL 0.107 -> 0.136 -> 0.210). A wider FOV helps consistently, naive history concatenation does not help (SR 46.8% no history vs 40.4-45.4% with history), and RGB-only navigability via Segformer loses only ~3 SR points while ZoeDepth loses ~10.
method: Navigability: builds a navigability mask from the depth image and computes, for every direction in the FOV, the farthest collision-free straight-line distance, giving polar actions A_initial.
Voxel map / exploration indicator: maintains a 2D top-down map from depth+pose, marking areas within 2 m as explored and the rest as unexplored; each action gets an explored/unexplored flag.

Action Proposer: builds A_final by adding unexplored actions with small angular spacing θ_δ, then explored actions with larger spacing θ_Δ, clips ranges to min(2/3·r, r_max), and adds a Turn Around (π,0) action when stuck (explore bias).
Projection: overlays each action as a numbered arrow/circle on the RGB image, with Turn Around annotated as 0 on the image side.

Prompting: a chain-of-thought prompt (system + task + annotated image) asks the VLM to describe the spatial layout, make a high-level plan, then pick an action; goal images are passed as extra input; the action is executed directly with no low-level planner.
Termination: a separate VLM prompt on the un-annotated image decides stop; the episode ends after two consecutive stop calls, and navigability/explore bias are disabled after the first stop.

setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (1080x1920, 131° HFOV, 25° downward pitch) + pose; goal as category name, image or text description
setting.action_space: discrete set of VLM-selected polar actions (rotation + forward displacement) chosen from proposed arrows, plus turn-around and stop
setting.privileged: none beyond simulator depth and pose; allow-slide enabled for main results (sliding past obstacles)

numbers.extra: allow slide on; success threshold 1.2 m; 131° FOV; depth sensor
allow slide on; Image SR 14.3, Object SR 20.5, Description SR 13.4
allow slide off; used for comparison with SenseAct-NN and Modular GOAT

numbers_note: ObjectNav split is not explicitly named in the text (likely the Habitat ObjectNav validation set), labeled 'val'. Paper prints SPL as decimals, kept as is.
results: VLMnav reaches 50.4% SR / 0.210 SPL on ObjectNav, beating PIVOT (24.6% / 0.106) by over 25 points, and 16.3% SR on GOAT val-unseen vs PIVOT 8.3%. With sliding disabled it falls well below specialized systems (6.9% SR vs SenseAct-NN 29.5% and Modular GOAT 24.9%).
limitations: Performance collapses without the simulator's allow-slide (50.4% -> 12.9% SR), since there is no backtracking and robot size/shape is ignored, so real-world collisions are likely.
VLM lacks fine spatial distance awareness (premature stops 1-1.5 m from goal in 13.9% of GOAT runs), and specialized systems still outperform it.
No memory usage: naive history does not help; evaluated only in simulation with Gemini Flash and near-perfect depth.
